conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the current best evidence from large, high-quality trials and an updated Cochrane review does not support the claim, noting that benefits are uncertain at best and likely minimal, leaning toward a negative conclusion.
conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
The evidence is actually mixed, and the most rigorous data now lean toward "no" rather than "yes."

Earlier meta-analyses (e.g., older Cochrane reviews, Lancet 2006 prevention review) suggested probiotics modestly shortened acute diarrhea duration, particularly in children in outpatient/developed-country settings. This supported the popular belief that probiotics help.

However, the updated 2020 Cochrane systematic review (Collinson et al.), which pooled higher-quality, larger trials, concluded that probiotics "may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts," with uncertain evidence on time to recovery, and found no significant difference in diarrhea lasting ≥48 hours or ≥14 days between probiotic and control groups (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub4/full; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8166250/).

This shift was driven largely by two large, well-designed randomized controlled trials published in NEJM (2018), involving nearly 2,000 children with acute gastroenteritis in North American emergency departments. Neither Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG nor a Lactobacillus/L. helveticus combination showed meaningful benefit over placebo in symptom duration or severity (https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2018/11/21/669373363/probiotics-found-to-be-ineffective-for-easing-symptoms-of-kids-stomach-bugs; https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/probiotics-not-helpful-young-children-diarrhea).

More recent reviews remain inconsistent—some (e.g., Frontiers in Pediatrics 2025) report modest benefit with low-to-moderate certainty evidence, while a 2026 pediatric emergency department review again concluded probiotics should not be routinely prescribed since they don't reduce diarrhea duration (https://emj.bmj.com/content/early/2026/07/29/emermed-2026-216212).

**Conclusion:** The current best evidence, especially from large, rigorous RCTs and the updated Cochrane review, does not support a "yes" answer. Probiotics' benefit for shortening acute infectious diarrhea is uncertain at best and likely minimal in real-world settings, contradicting the assumption in the original question.
